name: Leg lengthening medical tourism

card.summary: Travelling abroad for cheaper cosmetic leg lengthening, with lower prices traded against follow-up-care and regulation questions.
card.aka: Travelling for LL; limb lengthening abroad
card.note: Complications can emerge after returning home, when follow-up care may be harder to arrange.

quick.overview:
Cosmetic leg lengthening is expensive in the US and Western Europe, so some prospective patients travel to other countries where packages are cheaper. Turkey, India and Poland are among the destinations named in discussions of cosmetic surgery tourism.

No studies specifically examine outcomes of cosmetic leg lengthening done abroad. Evidence on medical tourism in general describes cost savings alongside risks around follow-up care, complaint procedures and travel after surgery.
quick.mechanism: Patients arrange surgery, often as an all-inclusive package, at a clinic in another country and stay for part of the lengthening period before returning home. The bone is lengthened gradually over weeks to months, so follow-up care continues long after the operation.
quick.risks: Medical tourism literature lists variable post-operative care, limited legal recourse, longer-than-planned stays and clot risk after long flights as concerns. Limb lengthening itself carries risks of nerve injury, contracture, healing problems and infection. Cosmetic limb lengthening is unregulated in some countries and has been banned in China.

lead: Leg lengthening medical tourism is travelling to another country for cosmetic limb-lengthening surgery, usually to lower the cost of gaining height. The surgery adds centimetres to a person's standing height by cutting a leg bone and gradually separating the ends so new bone forms; looksmaxxing and height-focused communities discuss destinations including Turkey, India, Poland and other Asian countries as alternatives to clinics in the United States and Western Europe.[2][3]

Medical tourism in general is described as travel abroad for treatment, driven by high domestic costs, waiting times, easier travel and improved standards abroad; cost gaps for some procedures are large.[3] Cosmetic surgery is one of its most common categories, with Turkey, Poland, India and Thailand among the destinations named.[3]

No published research has examined outcomes of cosmetic leg lengthening performed abroad. This article therefore draws on general medical tourism sources and on encyclopedia summaries of limb lengthening.

chain: Patient travels abroad for a package price
Leg bones are surgically lengthened by gradual distraction
Taller standing height and altered proportions after healing
angle.text: Travel lowers the price of a procedure that adds height by lengthening the femur and/or tibia. The patient trades the cost saving against being away from home for part of a long recovery.

infobox: Distraction osteogenesis of femur and/or tibia
About 2 to 3 months in package arrangements

paras: Limb lengthening cuts a leg bone and gradually separates the ends, at a rate commonly given as about 1 mm per day in two steps, after a latency of about a week; the bone is then held stable during consolidation until it heals and, with an external device, a second surgery removes the hardware.[2][4] Motorised implantable nails such as the Fitbone are associated with accurate correction, less scarring and lower infection risk than external devices.[1][4] Because the lengthening and consolidation phases last months, a patient who travels abroad either stays for a long period or returns home partway through treatment.

A Grokipedia summary reports that cosmetic lengthening is most available in high-income countries but is growing in popularity in India and Turkey through medical tourism, that Turkish all-inclusive packages typically involve a stay of two to three months, and that US prices are cited in the range of tens of thousands of dollars.[2] These figures come from an AI-generated source and have not been independently verified.

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed the approach in 1869 and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, with high complication rates; Gavriil Ilizarov's work from the 1950s on external fixation and separation rates led to its widespread use.[1][4]

Wikipedia reports that cosmetic limb lengthening in India is in high demand and unregulated, that some young patients have had infections needing further surgery or gained less height than expected, that some surgeons were said to understate risks, and that China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects.[1][4]

On medical tourism generally, Wikipedia notes Turkey's International Health Tourism regulation (2017) and the role of international accreditation bodies such as Joint Commission International.[3] Grokipedia states that the professional society ISAPS has cautioned against cosmetic procedures at unlicensed facilities abroad.[2]

Wikipedia's medical tourism article lists exposure to unfamiliar infections, variable quality of post-operative care, increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism after long flights, longer-than-planned stays when complications arise, and limited complaint procedures and legal recourse. It notes patients may find it hard to obtain follow-up care or insurance coverage at home.[3]

For distraction osteogenesis itself, Wikipedia cites infection in about 5 percent of cases, bone growing in the wrong direction in 7 to 9 percent, hardware failure in 3 to 4.5 percent, plus nerve injury, and notes that pulling too fast can cause nonunion while too slowly can allow premature union.[4]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes bone lengthening.[1][4]
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempt.[1][4]
Gavriil Ilizarov begins the work that leads to widespread use.[4]
China's Ministry of Health bans limb lengthening after operations with serious side effects.[1]
Turkey's Regulation on International Health Tourism takes effect.[3]
